[Session begins. Client enters.]
Welcome back. I just want to say — coming back for a second session, that means something. A lot of people don't make it back.

Yeah, well... I said I'd come back, so. [pause] I keep my word. At least I've got that.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:moderate]
What's been on your mind since we last spoke?

I don't know. Same stuff, I guess. It's been a rough week. My ex is trying to change the visitation schedule again, so I've been... I mean, I had a few more drinks than I probably should've. But that's just — the stress has been a lot, you know?
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:moderate]
So right when you're trying to find your footing, she changes the ground under you again.

Exactly! I mean, what am I supposed to do? She just — she does whatever she wants and I'm just supposed to sit there and take it? So yeah, I had some drinks. Sue me. That's not a crime.
[emotion:frustrated, defensiveness:moderate]
When you say you had some drinks this week — what does a rough week look like for you lately?

I don't know, like... five, six beers a night maybe. More on weekends. But I'm not like, falling down drunk. I go to work every single day. I'm functional. That's not — that's not the same as having a problem.
[emotion:frustrated, defensiveness:moderate]
You want me to know you're still holding things together. And I hear that. I also hear something else underneath it — it sounds like it's just... exhausting. Carrying all of this.

... [long pause] Yeah. Yeah, it is. I get home and the place is just — it's so goddamn quiet. The kids used to be there every other week, and now she's talking about moving them further away, and I just... I don't know what to do with that.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]
You're still showing up for them even when everything around you is falling apart. That's not a small thing.

I try to. I don't know if I'm doing a good job of it though. My oldest — she's sixteen — she called me last week and I could just tell, you know, she was worried about me. And that... that hit different. That hit hard.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]
What was it like to hear that from her?

Awful. She shouldn't — she shouldn't have to worry about me. I'm the parent. I'm supposed to be the one who... [voice breaks] I'm not doing a great job of that lately. I really haven't been.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]

Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You came back today because you keep your word — that's who you are. You're holding down a job, you're trying to stay in your kids' lives. And at the same time, the drinking has gotten heavier since the divorce, the house feels empty in a way that's hard to sit with, and your daughter's worry cut right through you. There's a lot of pain underneath all of this anger.

... [quietly] Yeah. That's... yeah. I didn't — I haven't thought of it all laid out like that but. Yeah. That's what it is.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
When you think about your daughter — about the dad you want to be for her — what comes up?

I want her to not have to worry about me. I want to be the guy I was before all this. I used to coach her soccer team, you know? We'd go get breakfast after games, just the two of us. I want... I want that back. I don't know if I can have it back, but I want it.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:low]
That wanting — that pull back toward who you've been for her — that's still in there. That didn't go away.

No. No, it didn't. [pause] ...Maybe that's why I actually came back. I don't know. Maybe I need to — maybe I actually need to do something about this.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

[Session begins. Client enters.]
Hey Marcus. I know this probably wasn't your idea to be here today, so I appreciate you showing up anyway. Can you tell me a little bit about what you understand about why we're talking?

I mean... my parents freaked out about some stuff they found. Which is whatever. They overreacted. I don't really get why I have to be here talking to some random person about it.
[emotion:angry, defensiveness:high]
So from your side, they blew it way out of proportion. And now you're sitting here on a call with a stranger, which probably feels pretty unfair.

Yeah. Exactly. Like... I don't know. It's not like I'm some addict or whatever. They found a couple bottles. That's it. Every kid does stuff like that.
[emotion:frustrated, defensiveness:high]
You're not some addict. Got it. I'm not here to slap a label on you, Marcus — that's not what this is. But I am curious — why hide them? If it was no big deal, why not just leave them out?

Because... I mean, obviously my parents would flip out. Which they did. So. That's just... that's just how parents are, it's not like — I wasn't hiding it because I thought something was wrong with it.
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:moderate]
You knew they'd react badly, so you kept it out of sight. That makes sense on the surface. Help me understand though — how long has this been going on?

I don't know. Like... since last year, maybe? But it's not — it's not every day or anything. Just like, weekends. When stuff is... when things are stressful I guess. Sometimes.
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:moderate]

Since last year. And it picks up when things get stressful. That's actually a really honest thing to say, and I don't think you realize that. A lot of people come in here and I never get that from them. What kinds of things have been stressful?

I don't know... school I guess. And like... my parents fight a lot. My dad kind of... he's been drinking more too, so it's like — whatever. It's fine. It's not a big deal.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]
Your dad drinks more when things are hard at home. And so do you. I'm not saying that to make you feel bad — I just want to make sure you heard what you just said.

...

Yeah.

I heard it.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]
That quiet right there — what's happening for you?

I don't know. I just... I don't want to be like him. Like, that's not — I never thought about it like that before. That I'm doing the same thing he does. That's kind of... messed up.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:none]

You don't want to be like him. That matters. That's not nothing, Marcus — the fact that you can see that pattern and it bothers you, that says something real about who you are and what you want for yourself.

I mean... I'm 16. It's not like I'm gonna end up like him. I can just stop whenever, you know? It's different.
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:low]

Let me be straight with you because I think you can handle it. He probably thought that too when he was 16. I'm not saying that's your future — I genuinely don't know. But "I can stop whenever" is worth actually testing. Have you tried?

I... no. Not really. I mean last month I went like two weeks without it and then my parents had a huge fight and I just... yeah.

Okay. Maybe I haven't tried that hard.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:none]

So let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You didn't want to come today, and you still showed up. You've been carrying a lot — a stressed home, your dad's drinking, school — and you found something that took the edge off. You're not stupid, you saw the pattern yourself just now without me pointing it out. And underneath all of that, you're scared of turning into something you don't want to be. That tells me there's a part of you that already knows what you want. What do you think a next step looks like for you?

I don't know. Maybe... maybe actually talking to someone. Like, actually talking. Not just because my parents made me.

Maybe I could come back next week or whatever. If that's — yeah.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

[Session begins. Client enters.]

Thanks for coming in today. I know walk-in appointments can feel a little... unexpected. Before anything else, I want to be upfront with you — nothing you share here gets reported back to your employer unless you're in immediate danger. So, with that said, what's on your mind coming in today?

I mean... HR said I had to be here, so. [pause] I'm not really sure what this is supposed to accomplish. I don't — I don't have like, a drinking problem or whatever. I just had a really rough night and I made a mistake at work. One mistake. In eight years.
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:moderate]
So this feels like something that was imposed on you, not something you walked in here choosing.

Exactly. Yeah. Eight years, not a single incident on my record. And now because of one thing they've got me sitting in a... [gestures around] I'm sorry. I'm not trying to be rude. I'm just — I'm frustrated. It feels like I'm being treated like I'm some kind of liability.
[emotion:anxious, defensiveness:moderate]

Eight years is a long time. And it sounds like that record matters a lot to you — your identity as a nurse is wrapped up in it. I'm wondering, and you don't have to have a neat answer for this — what do you think changed?

The pandemic. I mean... what do you think? [quieter] I held phones up to people's faces so they could say goodbye to their families. Over and over. And then you go home. And you're supposed to just... sleep? The drinking started because it was the only thing that actually turned my brain off. Like, nothing else worked. Not exercise, not whatever, not meditation apps. [pause] So.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:moderate]
It became your off switch.

Yeah. [pause] Yeah, that's... that's actually exactly what it is. And I know how that sounds — I'm a nurse. I know what alcohol does, I've seen cirrhosis, I know. But after a shift where you coded three people and only one made it back... a glass of wine stopped cutting it a long time ago. I needed to actually stop feeling things for a few hours.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:low]

You've been carrying a weight that most people genuinely can't imagine. And the drinking has been how you've survived it, night after night. I want to ask you about the incident at work — when that moment happened, when you caught yourself, what was going through your head?

I was... I couldn't think straight. Not like tired-tired, like — my brain wasn't tracking. And I caught it, I caught the med error before anything happened to the patient. But in that second I just... I knew. I knew I wasn't okay. [voice wavers] I've never felt like that at work before. Not once. That scared me more than anything HR said afterward.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
Even in that moment — foggy, exhausted, scared — you caught it. The part of you that became a nurse to protect people was still there, still working. That's not nothing.

I don't know if I deserve credit for that, I — [exhales] But yeah. It scared me because nursing is the only thing I've ever actually wanted to do. Like, since I was a kid. If I lose that... [trails off] I can't lose that.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]

Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and tell me if I'm getting it wrong. You went through something genuinely traumatic during the pandemic — things that would knock anyone sideways. Drinking became a way to survive those nights, to function. And now there's a part of you that's frightened, because you're starting to see it bleeding into the one thing that defines you — your patients, your work, who you are when you put that badge on.

When you say it like that... yeah. [long pause] Yeah, that's it. I think I've been telling myself it's fine, it's under control, because I couldn't let myself look at it directly. But it's... it's affecting my work now. I know that. I think I've known that for a while and just kept not dealing with it.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
What would it look like for you to get that version of yourself back — the one who goes home after a hard shift and can actually rest?

God. [soft, surprised laugh] I haven't let myself think about that in... I don't even know how long. I think it would mean waking up and not already feeling behind. Being actually present with my patients, not just going through the motions. Maybe not dreading going in. [quieter] I used to love going in.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:low]

That person — the one who loved going in — she's still in there. What you're describing isn't who you've become, it's what happened to you. And you're still fighting for your patients even now. That's who you are.

I... yeah. [quietly] I think I needed to hear that. I don't know where to start, but I — I want to figure this out. For real. Not because HR sent me here. Because I don't want to lose myself in this.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

You came in today not knowing what to expect, maybe thinking this was just a box to check. And somewhere in this hour, something shifted — you named what this has been costing you, and what you want back. That takes real honesty. So, thinking about what's actually realistic for you right now — what feels like a possible first step, even a small one?

I think... coming back. Regularly, not just once. I don't think one conversation is going to fix eight years of — whatever this is. And maybe looking into whether there's like, a program or something structured. I don't want to try to do this alone. That feels scary. But like... doable-scary? Not impossible-scary. Which is kind of new.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

[Session begins. Client enters.]
You just came through five days of detox. That takes something out of a person. What was it that got you through the door today?

Honestly? My brother basically dragged me here. I don't... I mean, I knew I needed to do the detox thing, that part I get. I was shaking bad. But I don't really know what I'm supposed to do now, sitting here talking to — no offense.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:moderate]
No offense taken. So the detox was necessary — your body made that pretty clear. And now you're here, not totally sure what this is supposed to accomplish.

Yeah. Look, I'm not some — I wasn't always like this. Four months ago I had a house, I had my kids every other weekend, I had... and then Sandra just — sorry. I don't know why I'm saying all this.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:moderate]
No, keep going. What happened four months ago?

She left. Twenty-two years and she just — she said she'd been unhappy for a long time. I didn't even see it coming, that's the thing. I just... I started drinking more, and then more, and I kept thinking I'd stop when I felt better. But I never felt better. So. Here we are.
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:moderate]
Twenty-two years. That's not just a marriage ending — that's your entire life getting reorganized around something that's suddenly gone. And you still walked through detox. That's not nothing.

I don't really feel like it's brave or whatever. I feel like... empty. Like what's the point. My kids are gonna grow up and their dad's gonna be the drunk guy.
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:low]
That image — being 'the drunk guy' to your kids — that one lands differently than everything else you've said.

It terrifies me. Jake is fifteen, he's already pulling away, and... yeah. That's the part I can't live with. Everything else, maybe I deserve it. But not that.
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:low]
What do you think it would take — for Jake, for that relationship — to not go down that road?

Showing up, I guess. Actually being... present. Not calling him when I've been drinking, which I've done, and I hate myself for it. Just being someone he doesn't have to be ashamed of. I haven't figured out how to do that yet but... I know that's what I want.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]

Let me see if I'm hearing you right. You didn't plan for any of this — the divorce blindsided you, and drinking became the only way to get through the days. But what's been eating at you most isn't even the marriage ending. It's Jake. The thought of him looking at you a certain way. You came through detox, you're sitting here, and when you talk about him, something shifts. That's still alive in you.

Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's right. I mean, I'm still angry at Sandra, I'm not gonna pretend I'm not. But Jake didn't do anything. He just has a dad who fell apart.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
You've got real anger, real grief, and a very clear reason to fight. What would it look like — three months from now — if things were moving in the right direction with Jake?

Maybe... showing up to his baseball games sober. Not just physically there but actually — he'd look over and see me and not have to worry. That'd be something. That'd be a start.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
You just described a very specific version of yourself — not perfect, just present and trustworthy. And you called it a start. That's a grounded way to think about this. Not all-or-nothing.

I always thought I had to fix everything at once and then when I couldn't I'd just... give up. Maybe that's been part of it. Like, maybe I can just try to not drink today. And then tomorrow. I don't know, maybe that's actually — maybe that's possible.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

So here's where you are: you came out of detox, you're not here because you have all the answers, you're here because of Jake. Because of who you want to be for him. There's real grief about the marriage, real anger, and underneath all of it — this clear picture of a dad who shows up. One day at a time isn't giving up on the bigger goal. It's how you get there.

Yeah. I think I can do that. I mean... I hope I can. But I actually — yeah. I want to try.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

[Session begins. Client enters.]
So, Marcus — can I call you Marcus? Your chart says a friend referred you in. I want to hear it from you, though — what's been going on lately?

Yeah, Dave basically dragged me here. I appreciate it, I do, but... look, I'm fine. The divorce was rough, obviously, but it's not like I've got some problem. I just — it's been a hard few months, okay? I drink a little more than usual, so what. I'm not falling apart.
[emotion:neutral, defensiveness:moderate]
A little more than usual. And Dave cared enough to pick up the phone and get you here. That's not nothing.

Dave worries too much. We were in the Corps together — he's always been like that. [pause] Look, Carol and I were together nineteen years. Nineteen. And now I'm in a two-bedroom apartment watching SportsCenter by myself. Having a few beers to unwind at night is just... that's what guys do. That's normal.
[emotion:neutral, defensiveness:moderate]
Nineteen years is a long time. What do you miss most — about the life you had before all this?

I... hm. [long pause] My kids. Tyler's sixteen, Maya's thirteen. I used to coach Tyler's baseball. Drive Maya to her violin lessons on Saturday mornings. Now I get them every other weekend, and even that — there's so much tension with Carol that sometimes the visits just... don't happen. And I can't — I can't make that happen from the outside.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
So the beers at night — it sounds like it started as a way to get through the quiet. But the quiet is also where all of that lives. Missing them. The Saturday mornings.

...Yeah. [exhales] Yeah, that's — I never thought about it that way. It's like the second they go home after a visit, I don't — I can't just sit there. It's too quiet. I open one beer, then another, and I'm watching ESPN at two in the morning and I don't even know how I got there. I don't even remember falling asleep.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
Even with all the tension, even when the visits fall through — you keep showing up for Tyler and Maya. That matters.

I mean... of course. They're my kids. [pause] Tyler asked me last month — he asked me if I was okay. He's sixteen. He shouldn't be worried about his dad. [voice tightens] That bothered me more than anything Carol's thrown at me. I keep thinking about that.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]
What was that like, hearing him ask that?

Awful. Like, genuinely awful. I just kept thinking — is that what he sees? Some guy who can't hold it together? My dad wasn't around. That was the one thing I swore — I swore I would never be that guy. And I don't know... [voice quieter] I don't know how I got here. I really don't.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:none]

Let me try to pull this together. You came in today because Dave — someone who's known you since the Corps — was worried enough to push. You've been drinking to survive some brutal nights in an apartment that feels too quiet without your kids in it. And underneath all the anger at Carol, there's a father who coached baseball and drove Maya to violin lessons — who is genuinely scared of becoming someone his son has to worry about. Tyler asking if you're okay landed hard. Because it meant something was showing.

Yeah. [clears throat] Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I think I knew things had gotten out of hand. I just didn't want to say it out loud. Saying it out loud makes it real, you know? But... yeah. That's real.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]
So if things did start to shift — six months from now — what would you want that to look like for you and your kids?

I want Tyler to stop worrying about me. That's the big one. And Maya's got a recital in May — I want to actually be there. Fully there. Not just... showing up. [pause] I think I need to do something different. I don't know what exactly, but — yeah. Something's gotta change. I can see that now.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

[Session begins. Client enters.]
I'm really glad you came in today. I know it can take a lot just to walk through a door like this, especially the first time... Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you here?

Honestly? My boyfriend. He gave me kind of an ultimatum — said he'd leave if I didn't get some kind of help. So. Here I am.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:moderate]
You came even though it wasn't really your own idea. That tells me something — maybe there's a part of you that's at least willing to see what this is about.

I don't know about that. I've done this before — the whole counseling thing — and it didn't... I mean, my husband passed away eight months ago, and I just... I drink sometimes. To sleep. That's all. It's not like I'm falling down drunk every night or anything.
[emotion:sad, defensiveness:moderate]
It sounds like the drinking has become a way to get through — especially since losing your husband. What's it been like, these past eight months?

Um... dark. I don't know how else to say it. I used to have this whole life, and now I just... I wake up and the house is so quiet, and I pour a glass of wine and it takes the edge off for a little while. I know you're going to tell me that's a problem.
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:moderate]
I'm not here to tell you anything. It sounds like that glass of wine gives you a few hours of quiet in a life that feels very, very heavy.

Yeah, well. The other counselors said that too — that they understood, that they weren't judging me — and then we'd do the exercises and the worksheets and... nothing changed. I'd go home and Gerald still wasn't there. He's still not there. What is any of this supposed to do about that?
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:moderate]

Nothing can bring Gerald back. And I think you already know that — and that's the hardest part of all of this. You've tried before, and the pain was still waiting when you got home. Of course you're wondering why this would be any different.

... Yeah. I just... I'm so tired. I'm tired of being sad, and I'm tired of pretending I'm okay, and I'm tired of feeling like a stranger in my own life.
[emotion:hopeless, defensiveness:low]
A stranger in your own life... can you say more about that? Who were you, before all of this?

I had friends. We had a garden — Gerald and I — and I used to host big dinners, I was the one people called when things were hard. And now I haven't... God, I haven't even called my sister in three months. I don't know why. I just can't face it. Any of it.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]

The woman who kept the garden, who hosted those dinners, who everyone called when things were hard — she's still in there. She's been through something devastating, but I can actually hear her right now, in the way you're talking.

I... hm. I don't know. Maybe. I used to think of myself as a pretty strong person. I always handled things, I was the one who held it together. And now I can't even answer the phone when my sister calls.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:low]

Let me see if I'm getting this right. You came in today, not really for yourself, but something in you showed up anyway. You've been carrying eight months of grief almost completely alone, in a house that's gotten very quiet. You've felt like a stranger to yourself — like the capable, connected woman you were has somehow gone somewhere else. And underneath all of it, there's a part of you that actually misses her. That woman with the garden.

When you put it like that... yeah. Yeah, I do miss her. I miss being me.
[emotion:contemplative, defensiveness:none]
That's something real to hold onto. If you were going to take just one small step — nothing dramatic, just one tiny thing — back toward that version of yourself, what might it be?

Maybe... I don't know. Maybe I'd call my sister. Or just... go outside. Gerald and I had a morning walk we used to do, same route every day, and I haven't... maybe I could do that again. By myself. I think about it sometimes.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

That's not a small thing. Imagining yourself on that walk again — without him — and being willing to even consider it. You walked in here today not sure what for. And now you're talking about morning walks.

I don't know if I'll actually do it. But... I think about it. And maybe that's something. Yeah. Maybe.
[emotion:hopeful, defensiveness:none]

Um. I just finished a detox program. Last week. They said I should, you know, follow up with someone. So. Here I am.
